entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="1Sam.27.1">1Sa 27:1</reference> <div eID="gen4141" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4142" type="x-p"/> The result of the last affair with Saul, after his life had again been spared, could not fail to confirm David in his conviction that Saul would not desist from pursuing him, and that if he stayed any longer in the land, he would fall eventually into the hands of his enemy. entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="1Sam.27.2">1Sa 27:2</reference> <div eID="gen4142" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4143" type="x-p"/> Accordingly he went over with the 600 men who were with him to Achish, the king of Gath. <hi type="italic">Achish</hi>, the son of <hi type="italic">Maoch</hi>, is in all probability the same person not only as the king <hi type="italic">Achish</hi> mentioned in <reference osisRef="1Sam.21.11">1Sa 21:11</reference>, but also as <hi type="italic">Achish</hi> the son of <hi type="italic">Maachah</hi> (1Ki 2:39), since <hi type="italic">Maoch</hi> and <hi type="italic">Maachah</hi> are certainly only different forms of the same name; and a fifty years’ reign, which we should have in that case to ascribe to Achish, it not impossible.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="1Sam.27.5-1Sam.27.6">1Sa 27:5-6</reference> <div eID="gen4144" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4145" type="x-p"/> In the capital of the kingdom, however, David felt cramped, and therefore entreated Achish to assign him one of the land (or provincial) towns to dwell in; whereupon he gave him <hi type="italic">Ziklag</hi> for that purpose. This town was given to the Simeonites in the time of Joshua (<reference osisRef="Josh.19.5">Jos 19:5</reference>), but was afterwards taken by the Philistines, probably not long before the time of David, and appears to have been left without inhabitants in consequence of this conquest. The exact situation, in the western part of the Negeb, has not been clearly ascertained (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.15.31">Jos 15:31</reference>). Achish appears to have given it to David. This is implied in the remark, “<hi type="italic">Therefore Ziklag came to the kings of Judah</hi> (i.e., became their property) <hi type="italic">unto this day</hi>.”

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="1Sam.27.7">1Sa 27:7</reference> <div eID="gen4145" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4146" type="x-p"/> The statement that David remained a year and four months in the land of the Philistines, is a proof of the historical character of the whole narrative. The ימים before the “four months” signifies <hi type="italic">a year</hi>; strictly speaking, a term of days which amounted to a full year (as in <reference osisRef="Lev.25.29">Lev 25:29</reference> : see also <reference osisRef="1Sam.1.3">1Sa 1:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.1.20">1Sa 1:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.19">1Sa 2:19</reference>).

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="1Sam.27.8-1Sam.27.9">1Sa 27:8-9</reference> <div eID="gen4146" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4147" type="x-p"/> From Ziklag David made an attack upon the Geshurites, Gerzites, and Amalekites, smote them without leaving a man alive, and returned with much booty. The occasion of this attack is not mentioned, as being a matter of indifference in relation to the chief object of the history; but it is no doubt to be sought for in plundering incursions made by these tribes into the land of Israel. For David would hardly have entered upon such a war in the situation in which he was placed at that time without some such occasion, seeing that it would be almost sure to bring him into suspicion with Achish, and endanger his safety. ויּעל, “<hi type="italic">he advanced</hi>,” the verb being used, as it frequently is, to denote the advance of an army against a people or town (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.8.1">Jos 8:1</reference>). At the same time, the tribes which he attacked may have had their seat upon the mountain plateau in the northern portion of the desert of Paran, so that David was obliged to march <hi type="italic">up</hi> to reach them. פּשׁט, <hi type="italic">to invade</hi> for the purpose of devastation and plunder. <hi type="italic">Geshuri</hi> is a tribe mentioned in <reference osisRef="Josh.13.2">Jos 13:2</reference> as living in the south of the territory of the Philistines, and is a different tribe from the Geshurites in the north-east of Gilead (<reference osisRef="Josh.12.5">Jos 12:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.13.11">Jos 13:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.13.13">Jos 13:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.3.14">Deu 3:14</reference>). These are the only passages in which they are mentioned. The <hi type="italic">Gerzites</hi>, or <hi type="italic">Gizrites</hi> according to the <hi type="italic">Keri</hi>, are entirely unknown. Bonfrere and Clericus suppose them to be the <hi type="italic">Gerreni</hi> spoken of in 2 Macc. 13:24, who inhabited the town of <hi type="italic">Gerra</hi>, between Rhinocolura and Pelusium (Strabo, xvi. 760), or <hi type="italic">Gerron</hi> (Ptol. iv. 5). This conjecture is a possible one, but is very uncertain nevertheless, as the Gerzites certainly dwelt somewhere in the desert of Arabia. At any rate <hi type="italic">Grotius</hi> and <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi> cannot be correct in their opinion that they were the inhabitants of <hi type="italic">Gezer</hi> (<reference osisRef="Josh.10.33">Jos 10:33</reference>). The <hi type="italic">Amalekites</hi> were the remnant of this old hereditary foe of the Israelites, who had taken to flight on Saul’s war of extermination, and had now assembled again (see at <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.8-1Sam.15.9">1Sa 15:8-9</reference>). “<hi type="italic">For they inhabit the land, where you go from of old to Shur, even to the land of Egypt</hi>.” The עשׁר before מעולם may be explained from the fact that בּואך is not adverbial here, but is construed according to its form as an infinitive: literally, “<hi type="italic">where from of old thy coming is to Shur</hi>.” עשׁר cannot have crept into the text through a copyist’s mistake, as such a mistake would not have found its way into all the MSS. The fact that the early translators did not render the word proves nothing against its genuineness, but merely shows that the translators regarded it as superfluous. Moreover, the Alexandrian text is decidedly faulty here, and עולם is confounded with עלם, ἀπὸ Γελάμ. <hi type="italic">Shur</hi> is the desert of <hi type="italic">Jifar</hi>, which is situated in front of Egypt (as in <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.7">1Sa 15:7</reference>). These tribes were nomads, and had large flocks, which David took with him as booty when he had smitten the tribes themselves. After his return, David betook himself to Achish, to report to the Philistian king concerning his enterprise, and deceive him as to its true character.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="1Sam.27.10-1Sam.27.11">1Sa 27:10-11</reference> <div eID="gen4147" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4148" type="x-p"/> Achish said, “<hi type="italic">Ye have not made an invasion to-day, have ye?</hi>” אל, like μὴ, is an interrogative sense; the ה has dropped out: vid., <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi>, §324, b. David replied, “Against the south of Judah, and the south of the Jerahmeelites, and into the south of the Kenites,” sc., we have made an incursion. This reply shows that the Geshurites, Gerzites, and Amalekites dwelt close to the southern boundary of Judah, so that David was able to represent the march against these tribes to Achish as a march against the south of Judah, to make him believe that he had been making an attack upon the southern territory of Judah and its dependencies. The Negeb of Judah is the land between the mountains of Judah and the desert of Arabia (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.15.21">Jos 15:21</reference>). The Jerahmeelites are the descendants of Jerahmeel, the first-born of Hezron (<reference osisRef="1Chr.2.9">1Ch 2:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.2.25-1Chr.2.26">1Ch 2:25-26</reference>), and therefore one of the three large families of Judah who sprang from Hezron. They probably dwelt on the southern frontier of the tribe of Judah (vid., <reference osisRef="1Sam.30.29">1Sa 30:29</reference>). The Kenites were protégés of Judah (see at <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.6">1Sa 15:6</reference>, and Jdg 1:16). In <reference osisRef="1Sam.27.11">1Sa 27:11</reference> the writer introduces the remark, that in his raid David left neither man nor woman of his enemies alive, to take them to Gath, because he thought “they might report against us, and say, Thus hath David done.” There ought to be a major point under דּוד עשׂה, as the following clause does not contain the words of the slaughtered enemies, but is a clause appended by the historian himself, to the effect that David continued to act in that manner as long as he dwelt in the land of the Philistines. משׁפּט, the mode of procedure; lit. the right which he exercised (see <reference osisRef="1Sam.8.9">1Sa 8:9</reference>). <reference osisRef="1Sam.27.12">1Sa 27:12</reference> is connected with <reference osisRef="1Sam.27.10">1Sa 27:10</reference>; Achish believed David’s words, and said (to himself), “<hi type="italic">He hath made himself stinking</hi> (i.e., hated) <hi type="italic">among his own people, among Israel, and will be my servant</hi> (i.e., subject to me) <hi type="italic">for ever</hi>.” David in the Army of the Philistines. Attack upon Israel. Saul and the Witch of Endor - 1 Samuel 28 <div eID="gen4148" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4149" type="x-p"/> The danger into which David had plunged through his flight into the land of the Philistines, and still more through the artifice with which he had deceived the king Achish as to his real feelings, was to be very soon made apparent to him. For example, when the Philistines went to war again with Israel, Achish summoned him to go with his men in the army of the Philistines to the war against his own people and land, and David could not disregard the summons. But even if he had not brought himself into this danger without some fault of his own, he had at any rate only taken refuge with the Philistines in the greatest extremity; and what further he had done, was only done to save his own life. The faithful covenant God helped him therefore out of this trouble, and very soon afterwards put an end to his persecution by the fact that Saul lost his life in the war.  <chapter eID="1Sam.27"/> <div eID="gen4149" type="x-p"/>
